title: New Dementia Cases Could More than Double by 2050
paragraphs: The number of people developing dementia each year could more than double around the world by 2050, according to a major new international study.

The study was led by researchers at the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at UNSW Sydney in Australia and published in the journal JAMA Neurology. It was carried out by an international group of research teams called COSMIC, which stands for Cohort Studies of Memory in an International Consortium. The researchers combined data on 38,418 people from 22 studies in 18 countries and territories across six continents. During the studies, 3,001 of these participants developed dementia.

Based on this data, the researchers estimated that about 11.4 million people around the world developed dementia in 2023. If the rate of new cases stays the same, this figure is expected to rise to 24.7 million new cases a year by 2050.

It is important to understand that these figures refer to new cases each year. Currently, around 57 million people around the world are living with dementia, and previous research has estimated that this number could reach about 150 million by 2050.

The study also found that dementia does not affect all groups equally. After adjusting for age, women were more likely than men to develop dementia, with 10.6 new cases per 1,000 people each year, compared with 8.6 for men. The rate was also much higher in low- and middle-income countries, at 13.6 cases per 1,000 people each year, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.
The researchers said that this is worrying, because many of these countries are aging quickly but have fewer resources to deal with the problem.

The study did not examine why the rates were higher among women and in poorer countries. However, the researchers have called for action to reduce risk factors, identify people at risk earlier and improve diagnosis and care. As Professor Henry Brodaty, one of the study's authors, explained, society cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond.
